approved: The majority voted against an amendment to the usual [second reading motion](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html), which is that the majority agree to the main idea of the bill (or, in parliamentary jargon, that the majority read the bill for a second time). The amendment was: > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House:* >> *(1) notes the Government's lack of support for, and failure to protect, Australian consumers; and* >> *(2) calls on the Government to reinvigorate the national Consumer Affairs Forum process, to enable the much-needed reform of Australian Consumer Law".* Because this amendment was unsuccessful, the original second reading motion will remain unchanged. ### What does this bill do? The [purpose of the bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6188) is: > *to introduce a national regime to regulate gift cards, including requirements that: gift cards must have a minimum three year expiry period; information about the expiry of a gift card must be displayed prominently on the card itself; terms and conditions cannot allow certain post-supply fees to be charged; and certain fees cannot be charged after a gift card is supplied.*

Labor supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Gift Cards) Bill 2018, which mandates a minimum three-year expiry period for gift cards, prohibits certain post-supply fees, and requires prominent disclosure of expiry dates. The speaker also moved a second reading amendment criticising the government's consumer affairs record.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Gift Cards) Bill 2018 introduces a mandatory minimum three-year expiry period for gift cards, aiming to reduce the estimated $70 million in annual losses from expired cards and address inconsistent state regulations.

The speaker supported the amendment to the Treasury Laws Amendment (Gift Cards) Bill 2018, welcomed the legislation as long overdue, but criticised its delayed start until 1 November 2019, arguing it should apply by Christmas. He noted that $2.5 billion is spent on gift cards each year, with 14% never redeemed, costing $74 million to 1.9 million Australians.

The speaker argued that gift card holders often lose value when businesses close, citing Toys R Us, and suggested funds from gift card sales be held in trust accounts. They noted that New South Wales and South Australia have enacted three-year expiry limits, questioned potential duplication between state and federal laws, and supported the bill as a step forward.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Gift Cards) Bill 2018 was defended as necessary consumer protection and "major economic reform," ending unfair gift card expiry dates and closing loopholes that allowed call centres in places like Tasmania to sell cards into New South Wales and South Australia, with praise for state minister Matt Kean and federal Minister Robert. The speaker criticised Labor's amendments to the bill, arguing the legislation was critical for all Australian consumers.

Labor supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Gift Cards) Bill 2018, which mandates a minimum three-year expiry period for gift cards as a compromise between consumer interests and small business needs. The speaker also endorsed a second reading amendment criticising the government’s lack of consumer protection and calling for revival of the national consumer affairs forum.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Gift Cards) Bill 2018 introduces a national minimum three-year expiry period for gift cards, requires expiry dates to be prominently displayed on the card, and bans post-supply fees. The reforms will take effect from 1 November 2019.
